facts.title: Born in a Darmstadt Lab
facts.text: Roentgenium was first created on December 8, 1994, at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany. The team led by Sigurd Hofmann and Peter Armbruster fired nickel-64 ions at a bismuth-209 target, and a single atom of roentgenium-272 was detected. The same lab also discovered its neighbors bohrium, hassnium, meitnerium, darmstadtium, and copernicium.

facts.title: Named After an X-ray Pioneer
facts.text: The element honors Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen, the German physicist who discovered X-rays in 1895 and won the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901. The name was officially approved by IUPAC on November 1, 2004, on the 109th anniversary of Roentgen's discovery. Before that it carried the placeholder name unununium with the temporary symbol Uuu.

facts.title: An Element That Vanishes Instantly
facts.text: Roentgenium is intensely radioactive and has no stable isotopes whatsoever. Its longest-lived known isotope, roentgenium-282, has a half-life of only about two minutes, while most others survive for mere milliseconds. This fleeting existence means every atom decays almost as soon as it is made.

facts.title: Made One Atom at a Time
facts.text: Unlike everyday metals mined by the ton, roentgenium has only ever existed as a handful of individual atoms produced in particle accelerators. The original 1994 experiment yielded just three atoms over many days of bombardment. Because so few atoms have ever been created, scientists have never accumulated a visible, weighable sample.

facts.title: A Superheavy Transition Metal
facts.text: With atomic number 111, roentgenium sits in group 11 of the periodic table, directly below copper, silver, and gold. Chemists therefore predict it should behave as a transition metal and possibly form a +3 oxidation state as its most stable, unlike gold which favors +1 and +3. It is one of the so-called superheavy elements, all of which lie beyond the naturally occurring lineup.

facts.title: Relativity Reshapes Its Chemistry
facts.text: In such a massive atom, the innermost electrons travel at a large fraction of the speed of light, triggering Einstein's relativistic effects. Calculations suggest these effects make roentgenium's chemistry diverge sharply from gold's, even though they are neighbors in the same group. This is a vivid reminder that for the heaviest elements, the rules of ordinary chemistry start to bend.

facts.title: Predicted to Be Denser Than Gold
facts.text: Theoretical models estimate roentgenium's density at roughly 22 to 28 grams per cubic centimeter, rivaling or exceeding osmium and iridium, the densest known stable elements. It is also predicted to be a solid metal at room temperature. These figures remain calculations, however, because no bulk sample has ever been produced to measure directly.

facts.title: Completely Absent From Nature
facts.text: Roentgenium is not found anywhere in Earth's crust, oceans, or atmosphere, nor has it been detected in stars or cosmic material. It is a purely synthetic element that exists only when human-built accelerators force lighter nuclei to fuse together. Any roentgenium that might have formed in the early universe would have decayed away billions of years ago.

facts.title: No Job Outside the Laboratory
facts.text: Because it is so scarce and decays in moments, roentgenium has no commercial, industrial, or medical uses at all. Its sole value is scientific, helping researchers test the limits of nuclear stability and the periodic table itself. Studying it deepens our understanding of how the strong nuclear force holds extreme atoms together.

facts.title: A Stepping Stone to the Island
facts.text: Roentgenium lies near the theorized "island of stability," a predicted region of superheavy elements that might possess unusually long half-lives. Each new isotope scientists create, including the relatively long-lived roentgenium-282, helps map the shoreline of that island. The hunt drives the development of ever more sensitive detectors and powerful accelerators worldwide.
